A.explanation: Final kinetic energy is about $47000 \text{ J}$, giving $v = \sqrt{2KE/m} \approx 14 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: This value results from an error in subtracting the $100000 \text{ J}$ of work done against friction from the initial gravitational potential energy.

C.explanation: This is close to the speed if friction were ignored, where all $mgh$ becomes $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $v \approx 24 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, not $31 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ - it overestimates the kinetic energy.

D.explanation: This mistakes energy for speed by omitting the square root, using $v = 2KE/m \approx 190$ instead of $v = \sqrt{2KE/m}$.

hints: Notice the two different distances: the vertical drop of $30 \text{ m}$ controls the loss of gravitational potential energy, while the slope length of $400 \text{ m}$ controls the work done by the $250 \text{ N}$ friction.
Connect the energies with work done: loss in $mgh$ equals gain in $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ plus work $F \times d$ done against friction.
Calculate $mgh - Fd$ to get the final kinetic energy, then use $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with $m = 500 \text{ kg}$ and take the square root to find $v$.
walkthrough: Start from rest, so initial kinetic energy is zero. The useful input is loss of gravitational potential energy for $m = 500 \text{ kg}$ falling $h = 30 \text{ m}$: $\Delta E_p = mgh$.
Substitute with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$: $\Delta E_p = 500 \times 9.81 \times 30 = 147150 \text{ J}$.
Energy is removed by friction acting over the slope distance $d = 400 \text{ m}$: $W = Fd = 250 \times 400 = 100000 \text{ J}$.
Apply conservation with work done: final $KE = \Delta E_p - W = 147150 - 100000 = 47150 \text{ J}$.
Rounded to two significant figures this is about $14 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. This is option A.
